original_question: Justify the observed tendency of generic two-dimensional Euler flows with small numerical viscosity to approach integrable point-vortex configurations, and design a dissipation model that produces this asymptotic integrable dynamics.
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies both parts of the paper’s exact open problem: (i) explain the numerically observed tendency of 2D Euler evolutions with very small numerical viscosity to select integrable point-vortex dynamics, and (ii) construct a dissipation mechanism for the 2D Euler equation that yields this integrable large-time behavior. It also correctly keeps the focus on generic 2D Euler flows rather than broadening to unrelated vortex or Navier-Stokes questions.
missing_details: The paper’s target is the incompressible 2D Euler equation itself, i.e. the velocity formulation ∂_t v + v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, rather than a generic statement about vortex models alone.
The motivating numerical observations are specifically on the two-dimensional sphere and torus; this setting is part of the nearby context for Problem 27.
The initial data are described in the paper as smooth and sufficiently general initial vorticity; your draft says 'generic flows' but does not mention smooth initial vorticity.

The observed mechanism is not merely convergence to an integrable configuration: smaller same-sign vortex structures merge into larger blobs, and the resulting blob dynamics is then approximated by point-vortex motion.
The paper emphasizes that the attractors are the integrable cases of point vortices, not arbitrary integrable configurations.

The nearby context specifies the concrete integrable regimes recovered numerically: 2 vortex blobs on T^2; 3 vortex blobs on S^2 for general angular momentum; and 4 vortex blobs on S^2 when the initial angular momentum is zero.
The dissipation part is narrower than your phrasing suggests: the paper asks for a model of dissipation in the 2D Euler equation whose large-time dynamics produces such integrable behavior.

To be fully stand-alone, the question should mention that 'small viscosity' here means very small numerical viscosity in the simulations, not an a priori physical viscosity parameter in a different PDE.

The surrounding discussion ties the problem to finite-dimensional approximations of 2D Euler by N-point-vortex systems and recalls the relevant integrability thresholds; your draft omits this context, which explains what 'integrable' is referring to in the paper.
refined_question: For the incompressible 2D Euler equation ∂_t v + v·∇v = -∇p, div v = 0, explain the numerical phenomenon observed for smooth, sufficiently general initial vorticity on the two-dimensional torus and sphere that, under very small numerical viscosity, like-signed vortex structures merge into larger vortex blobs whose effective point-vortex dynamics is driven into an integrable regime—namely, 2 blobs on T^2, 3 blobs on S^2 for general angular momentum, and 4 blobs on S^2 when the initial angular momentum is zero—so that integrable point-vortex cases act as attractors for the large-time Euler dynamics. Then construct a dissipation model within the 2D Euler equation whose long-time evolution produces this same asymptotic integrable point-vortex dynamics.
justification: The draft is essentially a paraphrase of Problem 27. The exact paper-faithful target is not a broader question about generic vortex relaxation, but the specific open problem in Section 10.2 asking for a justification of the observed attraction to integrable point-vortex cases and for a dissipation model in the 2D Euler equation that reproduces this large-time selection. The nearby context on the same pages defines what 'integrable' refers to here by recalling the finite-dimensional N-point-vortex approximations and listing the integrable cases on T^2, R^2, and S^2, then describing the torus/sphere simulations in which same-sign blobs merge until the effective dynamics becomes integrable. This makes Problem 27, not any earlier general discussion, the exact statement your draft is trying to capture.
